q: You're driving along a road and see this sign. What does it tell you?
options: No stopping for the next 100 yards
A 'Stop' line is 100 yards ahead
A level crossing is 100 yards ahead
Give way to traffic for 100 yards
explain: This sign warns of the distance to a 'Stop' line ahead. When you reach it, you MUST stop behind the line and wait for a safe gap in the traffic before you move off.

q: You're about to emerge from a side road at a junction with this sign. Who MUST you give way to?
options: Only vehicles that are signalling
Only traffic coming from your left
Traffic on the main road
Nobody, if you're turning left
explain: This is a 'Give Way' sign. You MUST give way to traffic on the main road when emerging from a junction with broken white lines across the road.

q: You're driving along a road and pass this sign. What does it mean?
options: There's no speed limit here
60 mph limit for all vehicles
End of minimum speed
National speed limit applies
explain: This sign means the national speed limit applies. It doesn't mean there's no limit – the maximum depends on the type of road and your vehicle, for example 60 mph for cars on a single carriageway but 50 mph if you're towing.

q: You see this sign at the side of the road. What does it tell you?
options: The maximum speed you may drive at
The minimum speed you must keep to
The speed advised for the bend ahead
The average speed of traffic here
explain: Signs with red circles are mostly prohibitive. This sign shows the maximum speed, and you MUST NOT exceed it. A minimum speed is shown in a blue circle.

q: You drive past this sign. When do the waiting restrictions within the zone apply?
options: At all times, every day
Only on Sundays and bank holidays
At the times shown on the sign
Only during school term times
explain: This sign marks the entrance to a controlled parking zone. The zone entry signs show the times when the waiting restrictions within the zone are in force. Parking may be allowed in some places at other times.

q: You drive past this sign into a residential area. How far does the 20 mph limit apply?
options: Only for the first mile after the sign
Until you pass a sign showing the zone ends
Only during school opening and closing times
Until you reach the next junction
explain: This sign marks the entry to a 20 mph zone. The limit applies throughout the zone until you pass the 'End of 20 mph zone' sign. Look out for pedestrians, children, cyclists and vehicles emerging from junctions or driveways.

q: You're driving along a road with this sign. What does the blue circle tell you about the speed shown?
options: It's the maximum speed allowed
It's an advised speed for the bends ahead
It applies to lorries and buses only
It's a minimum speed
explain: Blue circles give positive instructions, and this sign shows a minimum speed. A speed limit shown in a red circle is a maximum that you MUST NOT exceed.

q: You're driving on a motorway and see this sign. What does the 40 in a red circle mean?
options: It's an advised maximum speed
It's the minimum speed allowed
It's a mandatory speed limit
It's the distance to the obstruction
explain: A speed limit shown in a red circle is mandatory, and you MUST NOT exceed it. This sign also shows that the left lane is closed, so you MUST NOT enter or carry on in it.

q: You're following a slow-moving tractor and see this sign. What MUST you do?
options: Stay behind it while the restriction applies
Overtake it only if it's doing under 10 mph
Overtake it on the left if there's room
Overtake it if the road ahead looks clear
explain: This sign means no overtaking. You MUST obey traffic signs giving orders, so stay behind the tractor while the restriction applies.

q: You're approaching a narrow bridge where this sign is shown. A car is coming towards you from the other side. What should you do?
options: Drive on, as you have priority
Give way to the oncoming car
Flash your headlights and drive on
Speed up to get across first
explain: This sign means give priority to vehicles from the opposite direction. Wait and let the oncoming car come through first.

q: You're driving along a road with this sign. Which vehicles may stop there?
options: Any car picking up passengers
Vans loading or unloading goods
Buses, but no other vehicles
Any vehicle for up to 2 minutes
explain: This Red Route sign means no stopping during the period shown – here, at any time – except for buses. You MUST NOT stop on a Red Route unless signs show that you may.

q: This sign is a blue circle with no red border. What does that tell you about its message?
options: It's warning you of a hazard
It's telling you what's prohibited
It's giving tourist information
It's giving a positive instruction
explain: Signs with blue circles but no red border mostly give positive instructions – this one means ahead only. Red circles are mostly prohibitive, and triangles mostly warn.

q: You see a circular sign with a red border. What type of message do these signs mostly give?
options: Prohibitions
Warnings
Directions
Positive instructions
explain: Signs with red circles are mostly prohibitive – they tell you what you mustn't do. Plates below signs qualify their message.

q: What shape are most warning signs?
options: Triangular
Circular
Rectangular
Octagonal
explain: Warning signs are mostly triangular. Signs giving orders are mostly circular, and direction and information signs are mostly rectangular.

q: You're following direction signs with a white background and a black border. What type of road are you on?
options: A motorway
A primary route
A non-primary or local route
A route to a tourist attraction
explain: Direction signs on non-primary and local routes have black borders. Motorway signs have blue backgrounds, primary route signs have green backgrounds, and brown signs show routes to tourist attractions.

q: You're planning to follow a primary route. What colour background will its direction signs have?
options: Green
Blue
White
Brown
explain: Signs on primary routes have green backgrounds. Motorway direction signs are blue, and brown signs show the way to tourist attractions.

q: You see this brown sign by the road. What does the brown background tell you?
options: It's showing a route for heavy lorries
It's directing you to a tourist attraction
It's showing a diversion route
It's warning of farm animals on the road ahead
explain: Brown signs direct you to tourist attractions, such as the zoo shown here.

q: You're approaching a junction on a primary route. The green direction sign has a blue panel on it. What does the blue panel show?
options: A tourist attraction is that way
A local route leads from the junction
A motorway starts at the junction ahead
The road leads to an airport
explain: On primary route signs, blue panels show that the motorway starts at the junction ahead. White panels show local or non-primary routes, and brown panels show routes to tourist attractions.

q: You're driving on a motorway and pass these markers on the left. What does each bar represent?
options: About 1 mile to the exit
About 300 yards to the exit
About 50 yards to the exit
About 100 yards to the exit
explain: These are countdown markers to an exit from the motorway. Each bar represents about 100 yards to the exit, so move into the left-hand lane in good time.

q: You're a learner driver practising in your family's car with a relative. You see this sign ahead. What should you do?
options: Join it, but stay in the left-hand lane
Take another route before the motorway
Join it, but keep below 50 mph
Join it if your relative is over 21
explain: This sign marks the start of a motorway. Learner car drivers MUST NOT drive on a motorway unless they're accompanied by an approved driving instructor in a car with dual controls.

q: You're driving alone in your car at 8 am on a Tuesday. You see this sign at the start of a lane. What should you do?
options: Use the lane, as cars are allowed in it
Use the lane only to overtake
Use the lane if you're turning off soon
Keep out of the lane at these times
explain: This lane is for high-occupancy vehicles carrying at least the number of people shown (here, 2 or more) during the times shown. You MUST NOT drive in it during those times unless the signs show your vehicle is permitted.

q: You're approaching a bus lane with this marking. How will you know whether any other vehicles may use it?
options: Signs will show which vehicles may use it
Any vehicle may use it when it's empty
Only taxis are ever allowed to use it
Cars may use it if carrying passengers
explain: Bus lanes are shown by road markings and signs that indicate which (if any) other vehicles are permitted to use them. Unless signs show otherwise, you shouldn't drive in a bus lane during its period of operation.

q: You're driving through a city where trams run along the road. You notice a diamond-shaped sign. Who is it giving instructions to?
options: Cyclists
Tram drivers
Bus drivers
Pedestrians
explain: Diamond-shaped signs and white light signals give instructions to tram drivers only. You MUST NOT enter a road, lane or other route reserved for trams.

q: A school crossing patrol steps out ahead holding up this sign. What MUST you do?
options: Slow down and pass behind them
Stop before you reach the patrol
Give way only if children are crossing
Drive on if the children are on the far side
explain: You MUST stop when a school crossing patrol shows a 'Stop for children' sign. You MUST obey signs used by school crossing patrols.

q: You're driving near a school and see amber lights flashing below a 'School' warning sign. What does this tell you?
options: The school car park is full
A 20 mph limit starts in 1 mile
Children may be crossing the road ahead
Parking is allowed outside the school
explain: A flashing amber signal below the 'School' warning sign tells you there may be children crossing the road ahead. Drive very slowly until you're clear of the area.

q: You're approaching a level crossing when these lights start to flash. What MUST you do?
options: Cross quickly before the barriers come down
Slow down and look for a train
Stop only if you can see a train
Stop behind the white line
explain: Alternately flashing red lights mean you MUST stop. At a level crossing, you MUST stop behind the white line across the road.

q: You're approaching a level crossing that has no barriers. The red lights start to flash. What does this mean?
options: A train is approaching
A train has just gone past
The lights are being tested
You may cross if you look first
explain: At level crossings where there are no barriers, a train is approaching when the lights show. You MUST always obey the flashing red stop lights and stop behind the white line.

q: You're approaching a junction and see this sign. What does it mean?
options: Traffic signals ahead
Traffic signals not in use
Level crossing lights ahead
No stopping at the lights
explain: This sign warns that traffic signals aren't in use. If traffic lights aren't working, treat the situation as you would an unmarked junction and proceed with great care.

q: You see this warning sign for a staggered junction. What does the broader line in the symbol show?
options: The road with the most traffic
The road with a lower speed limit
The road that has priority
The road that's a dead end
explain: On junction warning signs, the priority through route is indicated by the broader line.

q: You see this sign showing a 20% gradient. How could the same gradient be shown as a ratio?
explain: Gradients on steep hill signs may be shown as a percentage or as a ratio – a 20% gradient is the same as 1:5.

q: You're on a road with these lines, and the broken line is on your side. You want to overtake. When may you cross the lines?
options: Only to pass a cyclist doing 10 mph or less
Never, as these lines ban overtaking
Only if the vehicle ahead waves you on
If you can get back before a solid line
explain: Where the line nearer to you is broken, you may cross the lines to overtake if it's safe, provided you can complete the manoeuvre before reaching a solid white line on your side. White arrows on the road tell you to get back to your side.

q: You see this warning sign with a plate below it. What's the plate for?
options: To tell you what the danger is
To give the distance to the next town
To show a temporary speed limit
To show the times the sign applies
explain: This is the 'other danger' sign. The plate below it tells you the nature of the danger – here, a hidden dip. Plates below signs qualify their message.

q: You drive past this sign. What should you be prepared for?
options: A 50 mph limit on the road ahead
Children playing in the road
A road with no parking at any time
Queues for a car park
explain: This sign marks the entry to a Home Zone, where people could be using the whole of the road – for example, children playing. Drive slowly and carefully, and be prepared to stop.

q: You see this sign. What should you do?
options: Speed up to get through the works quickly
Change lanes to pass queuing traffic
Take extra care and look for further signs
Watch the road workers instead of the road
explain: This sign warns of road works. Take extra care and look for additional signs giving more specific instructions. Concentrate on the road ahead, not the road works.

q: You see this sign on the approach to road works. What does it tell you about the speed limit ahead?
options: You MUST NOT exceed it
It's only advice and can be ignored
It applies only when workers are present
It applies only to large goods vehicles
explain: This sign warns of a mandatory speed limit ahead. At road works you MUST NOT exceed any temporary maximum speed limit.

q: You've moved over to pass a works vehicle showing this sign. When should you move back into the lane it's closing?
options: As soon as you draw level with it
When traffic behind starts to pass
Only when you can see it's safe
After you pass the next junction
explain: Where a works vehicle shows a 'Keep Left' or 'Keep Right' sign on the back, you MUST pass it on the side indicated. Don't return to the closed lane until you can see it's safe to do so.

q: At road works, a worker is holding this sign facing you. What MUST you do?
options: Drive on slowly past the worker
Stop only if traffic is coming towards you
Give way to oncoming traffic, then go
Stop and wait until you're shown 'GO'
explain: This is a manually operated temporary 'STOP' sign. You MUST obey temporary signs, so stop and wait. When the 'GO' sign is shown, proceed with care.

q: The broken white line along the centre of the road changes to this pattern, with longer lines and shorter gaps. What does this tell you?
options: There's a hazard ahead
You're entering a 30 mph area
You're now allowed to overtake
The road ahead is one-way
explain: When a centre line lengthens and the gaps shorten, it's a hazard warning line. Don't cross it unless you can see the road is clear and you want to overtake or turn off.

q: You're driving on a road with these lines, and the solid line is nearest to you. When may you cross it to overtake?
options: To pass a car travelling below 30 mph
To pass a cyclist going at 10 mph or less
Whenever you can see the road ahead is clear
To pass any vehicle that's signalling left
explain: You MUST NOT cross or straddle a solid line nearest you. But you may cross it, if the road is clear, to pass a stationary vehicle or to overtake a pedal cycle, horse or road maintenance vehicle travelling at 10 mph or less.

q: You're on a road with these markings, and the broken line is on your side. You want to park. What does the Highway Code say?
options: You may park, as your line is broken
You MUST NOT park where these lines are
You may park for up to 20 minutes
You may park, but only at night
explain: You MUST NOT stop or park on a road marked with double white lines, even when a broken white line is on your side, except to pick up or set down passengers, or to load or unload goods.

q: You're driving along a road with this area of white diagonal stripes, bordered by broken white lines. What should you do?
options: Drive in it to pass slow traffic
Use it to park if you need to
Use it as an extra lane at busy times
Keep out unless it's necessary and safe
explain: Hatch markings separate traffic lanes or protect traffic turning right. If the area is bordered by a broken white line, you shouldn't enter it unless it's necessary and you can see it's safe to do so.

q: There's an area of white chevrons painted on the road, bordered by a solid white line. When may you drive into it?
options: Only in an emergency
To overtake a slow vehicle
When you're turning right
When traffic is queuing
explain: If an area is marked with chevrons and bordered by solid white lines, you MUST NOT enter it except in an emergency.

q: You're driving at night on a road with reflective studs. What do white studs mark?
options: The left-hand edge of the road
The edge of the central reservation
The lanes or the middle of the road
The edge at lay-bys and slip roads
explain: White studs mark the lanes or the middle of the road. Red studs mark the left edge, amber studs mark the central reservation and green studs mark the edge of the main carriageway at lay-bys and slip roads.

q: You want to drop off a passenger on a road with these lines. There are no loading restrictions. What are you allowed to do?
options: Park for up to 20 minutes
Stop while your passenger gets out
Wait as long as you stay in the car
Park with your hazard lights on
explain: Double yellow lines mean no waiting at any time. You may stop while passengers board or alight, and to load or unload unless there are also loading restrictions.

q: The plate next to this yellow line shows times but no days. When does the waiting restriction apply?
options: Monday to Friday only, except Bank Holidays
Monday to Saturday only
Every day except Sundays and Bank Holidays
Every day, including Sundays and Bank Holidays
explain: If no days are shown on the signs, the restrictions are in force every day, including Sundays and Bank Holidays. Always check the times shown on the plates.

q: You're driving along a Red Route marked with these lines. You aren't a taxi driver and don't hold a Blue Badge. When may you stop to let a passenger out?
options: Not at any time
Only outside peak hours
For up to two minutes
Only on Sundays
explain: On Red Routes, double red lines ALWAYS mean no stopping at any time. This includes stopping to let passengers board or alight, unless you're driving a licensed taxi or hold a Blue Badge.

q: You see this bay marked in red on a Red Route. What does the red marking tell you?
options: It's available all day for the purpose shown
It's reserved for Blue Badge holders only
It may only be available for part of the day
It's a taxi rank at all times
explain: On Red Routes, a box marked in red may only be available for the purpose specified for part of the day, such as between busy peak periods. A box marked in white is available throughout the day.

q: You see these yellow marks on the kerb. Which of these is still allowed?
options: Loading goods for up to 20 minutes
Stopping to let a passenger get out
Unloading heavy shopping
Parking for up to an hour
explain: Double kerb marks mean no loading or unloading at any time. You may still stop while passengers board or alight.

q: You're collecting a child from school and see these markings outside the entrance. What should you do?
options: Stop on them briefly to pick up your child
Wait on them with your engine running
Keep them clear and stop somewhere else
Park on them if there are no other spaces
explain: These markings mean keep the school entrance clear of stationary vehicles, even if picking up or setting down children. Where upright signs show a ban on stopping, you MUST NOT stop on them.

q: You want to park in this marked area for a few minutes while you visit a shop. What should you do?
options: Park, as long as no bus is in sight
Park for no more than five minutes
Park with your hazard lights on
Find somewhere else to park
explain: This marking shows a bus stop. Don't stop or park at or near a bus or tram stop.

q: You're approaching a box junction like this at a signalled roundabout. When may you enter the box?
options: Only if you can cross it without stopping
Whenever the traffic lights are green
When you're waiting to turn right
When the traffic ahead is moving
explain: At signalled roundabouts you MUST NOT enter a box junction unless you can cross over it completely without stopping. At other box junctions, you may wait in the box to turn right if you're only stopped by oncoming traffic or other vehicles waiting to turn right.

q: You want to turn right at a box junction. Your exit road is clear, but oncoming traffic is stopping you from turning. May you enter the box and wait?
options: No, never enter until you can clear it
Only if the traffic lights are red
Yes, you may wait in the box to turn
Only if you're driving a large vehicle
explain: You MUST NOT enter a box junction until your exit road or lane is clear. But you may enter the box and wait when you want to turn right and are only stopped by oncoming traffic or other vehicles waiting to turn right.

q: Traffic ahead is queuing, and the only space left for you is on these markings. What should you do?
options: Stop on them, as the queue will soon move
Stop on them with your hazard lights on
Stop on them if no one is waiting to pull out
Wait before them until there's space beyond
explain: These markings mean don't block that part of the carriageway. Wait before them until there's room for you beyond, so the area stays clear.

q: A car ahead of you is showing this signal. What does it mean?
options: The driver intends to reverse
The driver is braking
The driver intends to turn left
The car has broken down
explain: Reversing lights mean 'I intend to reverse'. This signal shouldn't be used except for the purpose described.
ref: HC Signals to other road users

q: You're driving along a one-way street and see this sign. What does it mean?
options: Buses must use the left lane
There's a contraflow bus lane
There's a bus stop ahead
Buses have priority at the junction
explain: This sign shows a contraflow bus lane, where buses travel in the opposite direction to other traffic. In one-way streets, buses and cycles may have a contraflow lane.

q: You're waiting at traffic lights that change to show this. What MUST you do?
options: Move off if the way is clear
Stop and wait until green shows
Go, but give way to pedestrians
Go if you're turning left
explain: Red and amber together also mean 'Stop'. Don't pass through or start until green shows.

q: The traffic lights show this and you want to turn left. Pedestrians are crossing the road you're turning into. What should you do?
options: Go, as you have priority on green
Sound your horn to warn them
Edge forward to hurry them across
Give way to the pedestrians
explain: Green means you may go on if the way is clear. Take special care when turning, and give way to pedestrians who are crossing.

q: You're waiting at traffic lights showing red, with this green filter arrow lit. You want to go straight ahead. What should you do?
options: Wait for the full green light
Go, as the arrow lets all lanes move
Move into the filter lane and go
Go if no traffic is coming
explain: A green filter arrow means you may go only in the direction shown by the arrow. Don't enter the filter lane unless you want to go that way – wait for the full green light to go straight ahead.

q: You see this sign. What does it warn you of?
options: A level crossing with barriers ahead
Trams crossing the road ahead
A level crossing without barriers ahead
A railway bridge over the road
explain: This sign warns of a level crossing without a barrier or gate ahead. At crossings with no barriers, a train is approaching when the lights show.

q: You've moved out of a motorway lane closed by this signal. How will you know when the lane is open again?
options: The lane will look clear of hazards
You'll have passed the next junction
A sign will show a speed limit or 'END'
Traffic around you will start using it
explain: A red X identifies a closed lane, and you MUST NOT drive in it. A sign will tell you when the lane is no longer closed by showing a speed limit or the word 'END'.

q: You see this signal on a motorway with its amber lights flashing, but you can't see any problem ahead. Why might it be on?
options: It's being tested by the operator
It applies to large vehicles only
It's left on from an earlier incident
There may be a hazard you can't see yet
explain: Motorway signals warn you of hazards ahead, such as an incident, fog, a spillage or road workers, which you may not immediately be able to see. Reduce your speed and be prepared for the hazard.

q: You're approaching a narrow section of road and see this sign. What does it mean?
options: You must give way to oncoming traffic
The road ahead is one-way
Two-way traffic crosses ahead
You have priority over oncoming traffic
explain: This rectangular information sign means traffic has priority over oncoming vehicles. A circular sign with a red border is used where you must give priority to vehicles from the opposite direction.

q: You're on a motorway where the hard shoulder is sometimes used as an extra lane. The sign above it is blank. What does this mean?
options: Use it at up to 50 mph
Use it only if traffic is heavy
Use it only to reach the next exit
Don't use it except in an emergency
explain: A red X or a blank sign above the hard shoulder means you MUST NOT use it except in an emergency. You can only use it as an extra lane when a speed limit is shown above it.

q: You're driving under lane control signals. What does a green arrow above your lane mean?
options: The lane ahead is about to close
You should change to the left lane
The lane is for buses and taxis only
The lane is available to you
explain: On lane control signals, a green arrow means the lane is available to traffic facing the sign. Red crosses mean the lane is closed, and a white diagonal arrow means change lanes in the direction shown.

q: You're approaching a junction where a police officer is controlling traffic. The officer faces you and gives this signal. What MUST you do?
options: Drive on slowly past them
Stop before reaching the officer
Turn left at the junction
Flash your headlights and drive on
explain: This is a police officer signalling 'Stop' to traffic approaching from the front. You MUST obey signals given by police officers.

q: A police car wants you to stop. How will it try to attract your attention?
options: Flashing amber lights from in front
Flashing green lights from the side
Flashing blue lights, usually from behind
Waving a red flag from the roadside
explain: Where possible, the police will attract your attention by flashing blue lights or headlights, or sounding their siren or horn, usually from behind. You MUST then pull over and stop as soon as it's safe.

q: You see this vehicle. On which roads do its officers have the power to stop vehicles?
options: Only on motorways and trunk roads
On all roads, including motorways
Only at roadside check sites
Only on roads in towns and cities
explain: This is a DVSA officer vehicle. DVSA officers have the power to stop vehicles on all roads, including motorways and trunk roads, and you MUST obey any signals they give.

q: You want to turn left at a junction controlled by a police officer. Which hand may you use to give this arm signal?
options: Your right hand only
Your left hand only
Either hand
Neither – use your indicators only
explain: This arm signal tells a person controlling traffic that you want to turn left. You can give it with either hand.

q: When should a driver use arm signals?
options: Only when turning right in the dark
Instead of brake lights in daylight
Only when a police officer asks you to
To reinforce your indicators if needed
explain: Arm signals are for use when direction indicator signals are not used, or when necessary to reinforce your indicators and brake lights.
ref: HC Signals to other road users

q: A vehicle ahead of you is showing this signal. What could its driver or rider intend to do?
options: Stop on the left
Move out to the right
Overtake on the right
Reverse into a gap
explain: This signal means the driver or rider intends to move in to the left, turn left or stop on the left. Proceed only when you're sure it's safe, as an indicator may not have been cancelled.
ref: HC Signals to other road users
